newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right warns anew of left's election chances.
newsitem.headline: French right warns anew of left's election chances.

text.p: Outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe issued a stern warning on Thursday that France's left-wing opposition could oust his conservatives in Sunday's parliamentary election runoff after taking a stunning lead in the first round.

The right's concern deepened as its last-hope plan for a new ticket bringing together socially minded Gaullist Philippe Seguin and ultra-liberal Alain Madelin came under fire from the Gaullists' own centrist partners and triggered opposition sarcasm.
In contrast, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, sounding increasingly confident of winning the premiership, started talking about his first moves if he achieved office.
Stock prices measured by the CAC 40 index on the Paris bourse were up 0.8 percent by midday after falling 3.6 percent on Wednesday on market talk of an impending left-wing victory.
Asked in a radio interview if the left could win, Juppe said: "Yes. Yes it can win, and everyone must understand that this is what is at stake."

But he added that the ruling conservatives too could win in the tight race for the 577-member National Assembly and denied they were overwhelmed by fear of losing. The centre-right had 464 of the seats when President Jacques Chirac called the early general election.

"I have seen the will to win, because we too can win. Victory is within our reach," said the unpopular Juppe who has been sacrificed by Chirac and has announced he will quit after the election whatever the result.
Jospin told the daily Le Monde the race was not over, but he said the right's campaign was "confused and in disarray" and he did not think the first round swing to the left could be reversed.
Jospin told newspaper Sud Ouest that, if elected, he would form a tight pluralistic cabinet reflecting the components of his alliance with Communists and Greens.

He said his first move would be to call talks next month on cuts in the working week to create jobs, and controlled wage rises to help consumers and revive the economy. He would later present a budget focused on jobs, education and research.
Jospin aides said his third move would be to discuss with European partners the conditions he set to join the euro.

While Juppe said a Seguin-Madelin tandem would be a good team because the two men agreed on the essential, Jospin called it "a weird yoke", and "an impossible couple, the least social, the most anti-European".

The National Assembly speaker, a former campaigner against the Maastricht treaty on greater EU economic and monetary union who wants to put jobs before budget austerity needed to join the planned euro single currency, and ex-finance minister Madelin, an ultra-liberal pro-European, campaigned jointly as the right's improbable saviours with Chirac's blessing.
But ex-defence minister Francois Leotard, who heads the Gaullists' UDF centrist partners, called the team a pie containing "a liberal skylark and a big piece of Socialist horsemeat".
"That doesn't work...We have to choose. We have perhaps reached this situation because we have not chosen over the past two years," he said.
Conservative leaders rained warnings on voters not to force Chirac to "cohabit" with a left-wing prime minister.
Ex-premier Edouard Balladur, who shared power with the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand for two years, said everything should be done to avoid cohabitation again.
Leotard ridiculed a situation in which the president would say "yes" to the European single currency, the prime minister woold say "maybe" and communist ministers would say "no".
"It lasts five years and it looks like it won't be smooth," he said.
